releaseNote.summary: Fewer commits per hop: task journal written once at completion, one state save on a finishing hop, no redundant IsLatest update, optional asynchronous commit for bookkeeping rows.

bookkeepingCommitReduction.description: The pipeline hop's unit of work is not transactional, so every bookkeeping write is its own autocommit transaction and its own WAL fsync. Measured on digital-investment at 14 starts/s: 48 write commits per start, write commands 3-3.5x slower than reads (4.4 ms vs 1.3 ms), 79 percent of a request's database time. Four changes cut the commit count without touching instance state, data or outbox durability. (1) Task journal, one write per task: StandardTaskPersistenceStrategy no longer inserts a busy InstanceTasks row at creation and updates it at completion; the row is inserted once at completion with its final status, business status, payloads and timings, or - on a retry that found the previous attempt's row through the ExecutionKey probe - updated set-based. A task interrupted by a crash leaves no row and is re-executed on retry, which is what the reused busy row led to as well. The only observable difference: functions/tasks no longer lists a task while it is running (status busy). (2) A hop that enters a Finish state with no OnEntry tasks no longer saves the state change in ChangeStateStep and again in HandleFinishStep; the single save in HandleFinishStep carries both. (3) InstanceDataWriteService acknowledges the demoted previous latest row in the change tracker after an append, so a tracked aggregate's next SaveChanges no longer emits a second UPDATE InstancesData SET IsLatest = false WHERE Id. (4) New WorkflowExecution:Bookkeeping:AsynchronousCommit (default false): when true, the task journal write and the transition record insert/completion run in a transaction that commits with SET LOCAL synchronous_commit = off - visible immediately, no fsync on the request path, flushed by the WAL writer or by the connection's next synchronous commit; a database crash can lose the last few hundred milliseconds of those bookkeeping rows only. The wrapper costs three extra round-trips, so it pays off where fsync latency exceeds roughly three network round-trips; measure before enabling. The local compose Postgres additionally runs with commit_delay=1000 (group commit, no durability loss), the recommended starting point for any environment where the runtime's many small commits contend.
